summary: This proposed standard defines an optional IS-IS TLV called CAPABILITY, made up of sub-TLVs, with which a router can announce its capabilities within an IS-IS level or the whole routing domain. It obsoletes RFC 4971.

eli5.summary: Routers can tell their neighbors what special skills they have, like a name tag listing what each one can do. This defines the tag in the IS-IS routing system.

subtitle: A generic IS-IS TLV that lets a router announce its capabilities to the rest of a level or the whole domain.

tldr.problem: IS-IS routers often need to learn what other routers in their level, area or domain can do, for example for MPLS Traffic Engineering, but the protocol had no generic place to announce this.
tldr.mechanism: The Router CAPABILITY TLV (type 242) carries a Router ID, one octet of flags and optional sub-TLVs. The S flag decides whether it floods across the whole domain, and the D flag stops it looping between levels.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 4971 and fixes the IPv6-only case by allowing a Router ID of 0.0.0.0 when an IPv6 TE Router ID sub-TLV is present. The sub-TLVs themselves are defined elsewhere.

today: RFC 7981 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2016. It obsoletes RFC 4971, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Routers Advertise Capabilities
sections.content:
Routers running IS-IS sometimes need to learn the capabilities of other routers in their IS-IS level, area or routing domain. The RFC gives three illustrations from MPLS Traffic Engineering (TE): discovering mesh-group membership, advertising Point-to-Multipoint capabilities, and advertising IPv4 or IPv6 TE Router IDs for inter-area traffic engineering.

Each of those needs its own sub-TLV, carried inside the IS-IS Router CAPABILITY TLV that this document defines. The mechanism is deliberately generic and is not limited to MPLS Traffic Engineering. Defining the sub-TLVs is outside the scope of the RFC.
sections.eli5: Routers sometimes need to know what their neighbors are good at. This RFC makes one standard place for each router to write that down.

sections.title: The Router CAPABILITY TLV
sections.content:
The TLV has a type of 242, a length of 1 octet, and a value that starts with a 4-octet Router ID identifying the source, followed by 1 octet of flags. Optional sub-TLVs, formatted as in RFC 5305, may follow. The length ranges from 5 to 255, and the sub-TLV part takes 0 to 250 octets.

Two flag bits are defined. With the S bit (0x01) set, the TLV MUST be flooded across the entire routing domain; with it clear, the TLV MUST NOT be leaked between levels. The bit MUST NOT be altered during leaking. The D bit (0x02) MUST be set when a TLV is leaked from Level 2 to Level 1 and MUST be clear otherwise. A TLV with the D bit set MUST NOT be leaked from Level 1 to Level 2, which prevents TLV looping.

The TLV is OPTIONAL, and more than one from the same source MAY be present. How an application uses it is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The tag has the router's ID number, a couple of switches, and room for notes. One switch says whether the tag may travel to far-away places, and the other stops it from going round in circles.

sections.title: Elements of Procedure
sections.content:
The Router ID SHOULD match the value in the Traffic Engineering Router ID TLV (RFC 5305). If none is assigned, it SHOULD match an IP interface address advertised by the originating IS. If the node does not support IPv4, the reserved value 0.0.0.0 MUST be used and the IPv6 TE Router ID sub-TLV (RFC 5316) MUST be present. A TLV with Router ID 0.0.0.0 and no such sub-TLV MUST NOT be used.

A router that advertises capabilities with different flooding scopes MUST originate at least two TLVs, one per scope. To prevent stale data, a system MUST NOT use (or leak) a TLV from a system that is not currently reachable via paths of the level in which it was advertised. The RFC's example is a Level 1 area that partitions, where one L1/L2 router would otherwise keep advertising an outdated copy.

An implementation SHOULD advertise an update in the same LSP fragment as the advertisement it replaces. Where that is not possible, the two fragments should be flooded as an atomic action. Receivers can use a holddown time before processing an update. If two copies from the same system conflict for a sub-TLV, which one is used is undefined.
sections.eli5: If a router's name tag is out of date, nobody should keep passing it on. Tags with different travel rules go on separate cards, and an updated card should replace the old one in the same envelope.

sections.title: Routers That Do Not Support the TLV
sections.content:
Routers that do not support the TLV MUST silently ignore it and keep processing the other TLVs in the same LSP. Routers that do not understand a particular sub-TLV MUST silently ignore that sub-TLV and process the ones they do support.

For domain-wide TLVs from L1 routers to reach the whole domain, at least one L1/L2 router in every area MUST support the Router CAPABILITY TLV. When leaking is required, the whole TLV MUST be leaked unchanged (apart from the permitted flag changes), even if it holds sub-TLVs the leaking router does not understand.
sections.eli5: A router that cannot read a name tag just passes it along without a fuss. Tags are copied exactly, even the parts the copier cannot read.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the opportunity to snoop on or modify LSPs is not changed. However, LSPs now carry more information about router capabilities, which would also be available to an attacker.

Specifications built on this mechanism need to describe the security considerations for disclosure and modification of their own information. If modifying capability information is high risk, an integrity mechanism such as those in RFC 5304 or RFC 5310 should be applied.
sections.eli5: Anyone who could already read the routers' messages can now also read the name tags. If that matters, the messages should be sealed so nobody can change them.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 4971
sections.content:
RFC 4971 only allowed a 32-bit Router ID in the fixed header of TLV 242, which is a problem in an IPv6-only deployment where an IPv4 address may not be available. This document says the Router ID SHOULD equal the Traffic Engineering Router ID TLV (134) if available, otherwise an advertised IP interface address, and that 0.0.0.0 with the IPv6 TE Router ID sub-TLV is used when IPv4 is not supported. Some clarifying editorial changes were also made.

For IANA, the TLV codepoint 242 was originally assigned under RFC 4971, and the registry entry now refers to this document.
sections.eli5: The old tag only had room for an old-style address. The new one has a way to say there is no such address, and it points to a newer kind instead.

viz.caption: FLAGS OCTET OF THE ROUTER CAPABILITY TLV

fields.name: D
fields.desc: Set when leaked from Level 2 to Level 1; such TLVs are never leaked back up.

fields.name: S
fields.desc: Set means flood across the whole routing domain.
